INTRODUCTION.


This Index to the Encyclopedia of Pure Materia Medica embraces every-
thing except Houat's " proviugs " of Anantherum, Bufo, Cubeha, Curare,
Kali iodatum, Piper nig., and Sarracenia, and Wolf's " proving " of Thuja.
These have been omitted, since it has been demonstrated that they are un-
trustworthy as pathogenesies.

We are of the opinion that a few other so-called provings are unreliable,
but as it cannot now be demonstrated that such is the case, they have been
indexed.*

Aconitum cam., JEthiisa, and Hypericum have been indexed from the
revised pathogenesies in vol. x, supplement. All corrections noted in the
work, especially at the end of vols, iii and x, have been observed. A few
others have also been made, and still others will be published when the
revision of the Encyclopedia, now in progress, shall have been completed.

The arrangement is strictly alphabetical : First, the part affected ;
Second, the sensation, conditioned or modified,

I. There is no more reason for grouping the main anatomical divisions
of the body in an index to our symptomatology than in arranging a diction-
ary or an encyclopedia by topics ; indeed, there is much less reason for so
doing. The general anatomical divisions in our Materia Medica are not
satisfactory as a basis for classifying symptoms. We venture to hope that
future standard works will present a new scheme free from theoretical ideas
concerning the physiological action of drugs, classifying our symptomatol-
ogy in a form which will permit ready reference, and enabling numerous
provings to be condensed. In this index the part affected will be found
by referring to its first letter; symptoms of the brachialis anticus muscle


* Some observations concerning these will be found in our forthcoming Stu^
in Materia Medica.

will be found under "B.," of the wrist under "W.," of the eye under
"E.," etc.

This localization of symptoms is carried out to the fullest extent; for ex-
ample, in back we may find, first, all the sensations of the back (in general)
alphabetically arranged from ache to weakness, then the various parts of
the back arranged alphabetically :

BACK. Above anus.

— Arteries of.

— Near axilla.

— Opposite bowels.

— Dorsal regpion, etc.

Under each of these subdivisions of the back the sensations or symptoms
will be found in alphabetical order, conditioned or peculiar as the case
may be.

If the anatomical region have a specific and indepeudent name, it is
placed by itself ; for example, thigh, cheek, hypochondrium, umbilicus, etc.

One important point must not be overlooked, namely, the sides. In the
chest, abdomen, back, and other parts, the numerous symptoms of the sides
are placed together under a special subdivision of the general part, and
when the particular side is specified, the letter " r." or " 1." follows the
drug. In those portions of the body which are paired, this subdivision is
unnecessary, as in thigh, hand, etc.

II. Sensations. — There are cogent reasons for grouping similar or even
contrasted sensations. The British Repertory has done this in a very satis-
factory manner ; we, however, have arranged them alphabetically under
the various headings, and have given numerous cross-references. Patients,
as well as provers, vary in their ability to distinguish sensations, and what
may seem to one only a sharp pain, may by another be distinguished as a
cutting or sticking, or may even be recognized as composed of several dis-
tinct and peculiar sensations. There will be little difficulty in running
over the list as here arranged. Even in large divisions, such as back,
much less annoyance will be experienced, we fancy, than if the sensations
were ai-ranged in groups with a supplementary section for sensations that
could not be classified.

A word should be said concerning pain and sensation, expressions often
used synonymously; for example, a ''cutting pain," a "cutting sensation,"
a " cutting," all of which mean the same thing. We have placed them all
under cutting, and whenever a sensation or pain has been expressed by an
adjective which could be used as a substantive, expressing a distinct sensation,
this has been so used and classified.

III. Under each sensation will be fouud its conditions and peculiarities.

The conditions are first given and arranged in three sections :

(A.) General Conditions: First, Time; Second, Circumstance.

The " time " is arranged by the hours of the day and night, the circum-
btances alphabetically.

(B.) Conditions of Aggravation : First, Time ; Second, Circumstance.

(C.) Conditions of Amelioration: First, Time ; Second, Circumstance,

A sensation conditioned will not be found in the list of drugs under the
unconditioned sensation ; but an aggravation or amelioration, repeats the drug
in the unconditioned section; for example, " aching in the morning." The
drug will not be found under the general aching, but o^\.\ among those
aching in the morning. While aching, < or > in the morning is aching
ALL THE TIME, and < 07' > iu the morning.

The peculiar sensations are arranged alphabetically after the unmodified
sensation ; for example, back, pain. All the drugs having simply pam are
given with the conditions ; then follow all the (P.) peculiar p>ains alpha-
betically arranged, each with its conditions.

Among these peculiar sensations will be found all modifications of the
original sensation, such as course and direction (always under the initial
region), alternations of sensation, etc.

Much explanatory matter has been omitted, but only when it was of no
value in defining the sensation.

It was intended to add to the Index a chapter of conditions ; but the
size of the work renders it impossible to arrange them properly. This will
be done in a separate work to be called the Book of Conditions.

In the preparation of the Encyclopedia and its Index, we have been
actuated by a desire to assist in making firm the foundations upon which
homoeopathic therapeutics rest. We have witnessed, with anxiety, the
readiness of prominent members of the homoeopathic school of medicine to
rather than from pathogenetic indications ; and with equal anxiety have we
noticed the indifference manifested concerning the origin of symptoms in
repertories and textbooks, provided only they served to illustrate the action
of high potencies. Inasmuch as the physiological action of drugs may be
obtained from high potencies, and the sick may recover while under such
action, it behooves homoeopathic physicians to act with caution and rest
their feet upon the rock of pure Materia Medica, and not upon the shifting
sands of "symptoms," gathered from sick and well alike.

As long as our knowledge of the action of drugs upon the healthy is
imperfect so long we are obliged at times {though rarely) to rely upon clini-
cal indications, and to this end we recommend the use of repertories which
contain such indications. A good clinical repertory is certainly a desid-
eratum, but it should not be confined to material derived from homoeo-
pathic practitioners. There are good observers in therapeutics, not horaoe-

opathists in name, and many works professedly empirical abound in clinical
points of value.

We shall be glad to receive notice of any errors in the " Index." We
have striven to make it exact, but such work can never be perfect.

HAHNEMANN, DR. S. Organon of the Art of Healing. By

Samuel Hahnemann. Aude Sapere. Fifth American edition, translated
from the Fifth German edition, by C. Wesselhceft, M.D. 244 pages.
8vo. Cloth, $1 75

This fifth edition of " Hahnemann Organon " has a history. So many
complaints were made again and again of the incorrectness and cumber-
some style of former and existing editions to the publishers, that, yielding
to the pressure, they promised to destroy the plates of the fourth edition,
and to bring out an entire re-translation in 1876, the Centennial year. After
due consideration, and on the warm recommendation of Dr. Constantine
Hering and others, the task of making this re-translation was confided to
Dr. C. Wesselhceft, and the result of years of labor is now before the ])ro-
fession, who will be best able themselves to judge how well he succeeded
in acquitting himself of the difficult task.

" To insure a correct rendition of the text of the author, they (the publishers) selected as
his translator Dr. Conrad Wesselhceft, of Boston, an educated physician in every respect,
and from his youth up perfectly familiar with the English and German languages, than
whom no better selection could have been made." " That he has made, as he himself de-
clares, ' an entirely new and independent translation of the whole work,' a careful compari-
son of the various paragraphs, notes, etc., with those contained in previous editions, gives
abundant evidence ; and while he has, so far as was possible, adhered strictly to the letter of
Hahnemann's text, he has at the same time given a pleasantly flowing rendition that avoids
the harshness of a strictly literal translation." — Hahnemannian Monthly.

HOMCEOPATHIC JOURNALS.


THE NORTH AMERICAN JOURNAL OP HOMCEOPATHY.

Samuel A. Lilienthal, M.D., Editor. Boericke & Tafel, Publishers.
Quarterly. Subscription price per year, paj^able in advance. $4 00

This is the oldest Homoeopatliic Journal in this country, being now in its twenty-seventh
year. The first volume was published in 1851, under the editorshif) of C. Hering, M.D., of
Philadelphia; E. E. Marcy, M.D., and J. W. Metcalfe, M.D., of New York. In 1856, E.
E. Marcy and J. C Peters^ M.D., of New York; Wm. H. Holcombe, M.D., of Waterproof,
La., and II. C. Preston, M.D., of Providence, R. I., appear as editors. In 1860, Dr. J. C.
Peters, with a corps of assistant editors, assumed charge; and from 1861 until 1869 the late
Dr. F. W. Hunt virtually edited the .Journal, although his name did not always appear as
mch. In 1870, Dr. S. Lilienthal became associated with Dr. Hunt as co-editor, and since
1871 Dr. Samuel A. Lilienthal took sole charge of the Journal.

The Journal had its ups and downs during the long years of its existence, but under the
administration of indefatigable Dr. Lilienthal it entered on a career of prosperity such lis it
never enjoyed before, and it is safe to say that it never before had as many friends, as ^lu-
able original or translated articles, and as large a subscription list.

The Tw-enty-eighth Volume of this Journal commences in August, 1879. Subscriptions
